lab.name: Bacteria & Mixed Cultures
lab.description: Souring bacteria and mixed fermentation cultures. These are not yeast — they are lactic and acetic acid bacteria that produce acid rather than (much) alcohol, plus the blended cultures that combine them with Saccharomyces and Brettanomyces. Catalogued at species level with the commercial products noted, because behaviour varies enormously by strain.

attribution: Species behaviour, temperature and pH tolerances compiled from published brewing microbiology literature and producer datasheets (Omega, White Labs, Wyeast, Lallemand WildBrew). Souring organisms are described by the acid they produce and the pH they reach rather than by attenuation, which is not a meaningful measure for them.

strains.name: Lactobacillus plantarum
strains.description: The workhorse of kettle souring. Fast and reliable — will typically drop wort from pH 5.3 to 3.3 in 24–48 hours at 35 °C, after which you boil to kill it and ferment normally with yeast. Produces almost no alcohol itself.
strains.flavorNotes: Clean lactic tartness, little to no funk.
strains.optimalPitchNote: Hop-sensitive: more than about 5–8 IBU will inhibit it, so sour the wort BEFORE any hop addition. Purge headspace with CO2 to prevent the butyric/vomit off-flavours that come from competing organisms in an oxygen-exposed sour.

strains.name: Lactobacillus brevis
strains.description: More hop-tolerant and more alcohol-tolerant than L. plantarum, which makes it the Lactobacillus of choice for long mixed-culture ageing rather than quick kettle souring. Slower to acidify but keeps working for months.
strains.flavorNotes: Lactic acidity with more complexity and a slight funk over time.
strains.optimalPitchNote: Tolerates roughly 10–15 IBU. A common spoilage organism in ordinary beer — segregate soft equipment.

strains.name: Pediococcus damnosus
strains.description: The slow, deep souring organism of traditional Belgian sour beer. Highly hop-tolerant and works over months to years, producing a rounder acidity than Lactobacillus.
strains.flavorNotes: Deep lactic sourness; substantial diacetyl during the process.
strains.optimalPitchNote: Expect a 'sick' or ropy phase — Pediococcus produces exopolysaccharides that make the beer viscous and snot-like, and heavy diacetyl. Both are normal and clear given time, provided Brettanomyces is present to clean them up. Do not panic and do not dump it. Effectively requires a Brett partner.

strains.name: Acetobacter
strains.description: Converts ethanol into acetic acid — it makes vinegar. Requires oxygen, which is the key to controlling it: in a sealed, full vessel it does very little; in a barrel with headspace or a leaky bung it will take over.
strains.flavorNotes: Vinegar, sharp acetic bite; ethyl acetate (nail polish) at higher levels.
strains.optimalPitchNote: Almost never pitched deliberately in beer. Traces contribute authentic complexity in Flanders reds; excess is a fault. Control it by controlling oxygen — keep vessels topped up and sealed.

strains.name: Lambic / Mixed-Culture Blend (generic)
strains.description: The full traditional consortium. Saccharomyces ferments the sugars first, Lactobacillus and Pediococcus acidify over months, and Brettanomyces slowly consumes the dextrins the others leave behind — which is why a properly aged lambic finishes near 1.000.
strains.flavorNotes: Barnyard funk, lactic tartness, citrus, leather; develops over 1–3 years.
strains.optimalPitchNote: Plan for a year minimum, three for gueuze. Use dedicated soft equipment — tubing, buckets, gaskets — and never let this culture near your clean beer.

strains.name: Brettanomyces lambicus
strains.description: The cherry-pie Brett. Distinct from B. bruxellensis in emphasis — more fruit and spice, less horse blanket — and traditionally associated with kriek.
strains.flavorNotes: Sour cherry, pie crust, clove, mild funk.

strains.name: Brettanomyces claussenii
strains.description: The mildest of the common Brett species — originally isolated from English stock ales. A good first Brett: fruity and restrained rather than barnyard.
strains.flavorNotes: Pineapple, tropical fruit, very light funk.

strains.name: Brettanomyces anomalus
strains.description: Less common Brett species used for added complexity in mixed cultures; sits between claussenii's fruit and bruxellensis's funk.
